name: King's Indian Defense: Petrosian System
summary: The Petrosian System meets the Classical King's Indian with 7.d5, closing the centre before Black's ...a5 and ...f5 counterplay.
intro: The Petrosian System arises after 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.e4 d6 5.Nf3 O-O 6.Be2 e5 7.d5, a restrained but ambitious way to meet the Classical King's Indian. Instead of castling into the sharp Mar del Plata lines, White resolves the central tension at once, gaining queenside space and denying Black the ...exd4 options available after 7.O-O. Black most often replies 7...a5, fixing the queenside pawn structure and clearing a6 for the knight, before pursuing the standard King's Indian plan of ...Ne8 and ...f5. Named after the ninth World Champion, Tigran Petrosian, the system reflects his trademark preference for prophylaxis and secure, space-based positions.
line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Nf3 O-O Be2 e5 d5 a5

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: By locking the centre with 7.d5, White fixes the pawn structure early and steers the game into a maneuvering battle on the wings. White gains queenside space and often continues with Bg5 to pin the f6-knight and hamper Black's freeing ...f5, combined with expansion by a3, b4 or Nd2 and pressure on the c-file. Black seeks the classic King's Indian counterplay with ...Ne8 and ...f5, and may reroute the knight via ...Na6-c5 to pressure e4 and the queenside. Because the centre is closed, both sides enjoy time to prepare, and accurate move orders and patient planning matter more than immediate tactics.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: The main line runs 7...a5, when 8.Bg5 is Petrosian's characteristic choice, pinning the knight and probing before Black can organise ...f5. Black may respond with ...h6 and ...Na6, heading for c5, or prepare the break with ...Ne8 and ...Nd7. A key alternative for Black is the immediate 7...Nbd7, developing flexibly and keeping the ...Nc5 and ...a5 ideas in reserve. Play frequently transposes among these move orders, and the resulting middlegames revolve around whether Black can generate enough kingside pressure to offset White's space.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The system is named after Tigran Petrosian, World Champion from 1963 to 1969, whose deep understanding of closed positions and prophylactic defence made the early 7.d5 a natural fit for his style. By shutting the centre, Petrosian denied his opponents the dynamic piece play they craved and instead invited a slow struggle he was superbly equipped to win. The line became a respected mainstay of Classical King's Indian theory and remains a practical choice for players who prefer to blunt Black's counterattack rather than meet it head-on in the Mar del Plata.
